summary: The note covers a series of four Saturday conservation workshops at Meadowlark Community Center, led by the grassroots group Green Eden and founded by Dr. Lily Hamilton. Homeowners learned practical skills in rainwater harvesting, energy efficiency, waste reduction and organic gardening from local experts. The article stresses community bonding and everyday actions as the foundation of local environmentalism.
one_line: Green Eden's four-part workshop series at Meadowlark Community Center teaches homeowners practical conservation skills, from rainwater harvesting to organic gardening.
key_facts: The workshops were held at Meadowlark Community Center, with the article dated October 12, 2023.
Green Eden, a grassroots organization, spearheaded the conservation workshops.
Dr. Lily Hamilton, a local environmental advocate, conceived the workshops to give homeowners practical know-how for conservation at home and in gardens.
The series has four interactive sessions held each Saturday since September 25, 2023.
Topics include rainwater harvesting, energy conservation, organic gardening and waste reduction.

Maggie Saunders, a local homeowner and mother of two, said the water conservation session was eye-opening: "I never realized how much water we wasted on a daily basis." She now has a rainwater collection barrel in her garden.
Each session begins with an expert presentation followed by hands-on activities.
James Erickson, an energy consultant, led the energy efficiency workshop, including a live demonstration of energy-efficient appliances and lighting.

John Thompson, director of the local recycling center, led the waste reduction discussions on composting and responsible consumption; he said, "It's not just about recycling what we consume but reconsidering what we buy in the first place."
Maria Gonzalez, a horticulturist, taught organic gardening without harmful pesticides, including planting seedlings and companion planting.
Participants include homemakers, retirees, entrepreneurs and students, and neighbors have bonded as "comrades in conservation."
Many participants are planning initiatives to encourage wider community involvement after the final session.
